main_html:
Root Canal Treatment

Educational only. Not medical advice. No endorsements or rankings.

Quick answer

Root canal pages should help people compare saving the tooth versus extraction, not just react to fear. The useful question is what the diagnosis shows, how restorable the tooth is, and what the long-term plan looks like after the endodontic step.

Good pages reduce panic and improve comparison.

Cost and what affects the total

The root canal itself may be only part of the number. Crown work, retreatment risk, specialist referral, imaging, and emergency scheduling can all change the real total.

Ask for the full care path, not just the procedure price.

Recovery and short-term expectations

People should know what discomfort is normal, when chewing should improve, what follow-up restoration is needed, and what symptoms mean the office needs to hear from them again.

A root canal decision is incomplete if the restoration plan is missing.

When saving the tooth is usually worth considering

Root canal treatment often makes sense when the tooth is structurally salvageable and preserving it is still clinically meaningful. It is a worse fit when fracture, severe breakdown, periodontal problems, or broader treatment realities make extraction more rational.

The page should help readers compare these paths soberly.

Questions worth asking before you decide

Ask questions that connect diagnosis to long-term outcome.

  • How restorable is this tooth after treatment?
  • Would an endodontist change the prognosis?
  • What happens if I wait?
  • What is the plan after the root canal to protect the tooth?

Red flags and trust checks

Be cautious if the office talks about pain but not prognosis, or if extraction and saving-the-tooth options are treated as emotionally loaded instead of clinically compared.

Trust rises when the office can explain both paths without steering you through fear.

The crown afterwards is part of the treatment, not an upsell

A root canal and the restoration that follows it are one project quoted as two things, and the gap between them is where most of the cost confusion and most of the failures live. A treated back tooth has had its interior removed and is more brittle than it was; it usually needs a crown, and sometimes a post or a build-up first, to keep it from fracturing. A fracture after successful root canal treatment is one of the more common reasons such a tooth is eventually lost anyway.

Ask whether the quote you have been given is for the root canal alone, and what the full figure is including the final restoration. Ask whether the same office does both or whether a specialist does the root canal and your general dentist restores it, since that is two fees, two appointments and two diaries. Ask how long the temporary filling can stay in before the permanent restoration must be placed, and put that date in your calendar: a tooth left under a temporary for months can be re-contaminated, which undoes the treatment you paid for.

If cost means the crown has to wait, say so and ask what the safest sequence is. There is usually a better plan than silence, and the office can only offer it if it knows.

Saving the tooth against removing it, honestly compared

The real decision is rarely root canal against nothing. It is root canal plus a crown against extraction plus whatever replaces the tooth. Compared properly, those two paths often sit closer together on cost than they first appear, and they differ far more on time, number of visits and what happens in ten years.

  • What the prognosis is for this specific tooth, in plain terms, and what makes it better or worse: remaining structure, root shape, previous treatment, cracks, and the state of the bone around it.
  • What the full cost and timeline of the save path is, including the crown.
  • What the full cost and timeline of the extraction path is, including the replacement you would choose.
  • What happens if the root canal is done and the tooth fails anyway: whether retreatment, surgery, or extraction would be next.
  • Whether doing nothing for now is a genuine option, and what the risk of waiting is.

Ask for both paths priced on the same page. An office willing to quote the option it does not perform is giving you a comparison rather than a recommendation, and that is the thing you came for.

Afterwards, and when to come back

Expect the tooth to be tender for a few days, particularly to biting, as the ligament around the root settles. Mild discomfort managed with ordinary pain relief, easing day by day, is the normal course. Some teeth flare up in the first couple of days before improving, and knowing that in advance prevents a frightening night.

What warrants a call is pain that increases rather than fades, swelling in the face or gum, a temporary filling that comes out, a tooth that feels high when you bite, fever, or a return of the original symptoms weeks or months later. That last one matters: root canal treatment has a good but not perfect success rate, and a tooth that was comfortable and then is not again needs re-examination rather than patience.

Ask whether a review appointment and a follow-up image are planned, and when. Ask what the office does if the treatment does not settle — retreatment, referral to an endodontist, or surgery — and whether any of that is covered by a warranty. Ask also whether the tooth will darken, which treated front teeth sometimes do, and what the options are if it does, since that is a cosmetic consequence nobody mentions until it has happened.

What to do next

Use this page to compare root canal versus extraction conversations with the same checklist: diagnosis, restorable status, long-term plan, total cost, and timing. City pages should route pain and decision-intent users here before they commit.

If the explanation still feels muddy, get a second opinion.

Root Canal Readiness Scorecard

Use this scorecard before booking root-canal care.

  • Why is root canal recommended instead of monitoring, filling, crown, or extraction?
  • Should an endodontist review this?
  • What imaging supports the diagnosis?
  • What restoration is needed afterward?
  • What is the full cost including crown or follow-up?
